title: Debugging Bash Scripts: Make the Shell Show Its Work
summary: A dense study-notes series on finding out why bash scripts fail: static checks with bash -n and shellcheck, execution tracing with set -x and PS4, automatic post-mortems with trap ERR, strict mode with set -euo pipefail, a field guide to common silent-failure patterns, and stepping through logic with bashdb.

chapters.title: Why Bash Fails Silently: The Debugging Mindset
points: Bash runs top to bottom and does not stop on errors by default: line 40 can crash after lines 1-39 already did their damage
Exit status contract: 0 is success, 1-255 is failure; $? always holds the last status — check it after critical commands
A pipeline returns only the LAST command's status by default, so failing_cmd | grep ... looks successful
Unquoted $var undergoes word splitting and globbing: filenames with spaces silently break loops and rm commands
Silent expansion horror: rm -rf $DIR/* with unset DIR becomes rm -rf /*
set -e is a seatbelt, not a debugger: it stops the script but never explains why
Standard workflow: reproduce, add visibility with set -x, isolate with bash -n and strategic echo, then fix and re-run
Send debug output to stderr with >&2 so it never pollutes stdout that gets piped or redirected
Run bash script.sh directly to rule out a bad shebang or the wrong interpreter being invoked
Version matters: associative arrays (4.0), ${var,,} (4.0), ${arr@Q} (4.4) fail oddly on old bash
Scripts often work in your terminal and fail in cron: different PATH, empty environment, no TTY — diff the environments
Golden rule: never debug by staring at code — make the shell show its work

chapters.title: Static Checks: bash -n and shellcheck
points: bash -n script.sh parses the entire script and reports syntax errors WITHOUT executing a single command — the safest first check
Exit code 0 from bash -n means parseable; anything else means do not run this script
Typical report: unexpected EOF while looking for matching quote — bash tells you where it gave up, not where you erred
Missing fi, done, or esac surfaces as unexpected end of file: search upward from the reported line for the unclosed opener
Hard limit: bash -n cannot see runtime problems — wrong variable names, missing files, and bad logic all parse fine
shellcheck is a static analyzer that catches unquoted variables, useless cat, unreachable code, and quoting bugs
SC2086 (double quote to prevent globbing and word splitting) is the single most common shellcheck finding
Use shellcheck -x to follow source'd files and -S error|warning|info to set the minimum severity
Inline directives: # shellcheck disable=SC2086 silences one known-safe warning without hiding the rest
CI gate: fail the pipeline when bash -n or shellcheck -S error exits non-zero — broken syntax never reaches prod
Editor integration (vim-ale, VS Code Bash IDE) runs shellcheck on save for instant feedback
Static tools cannot know what variables HOLD at runtime — that is what tracing (set -x) is for

chapters.title: set -x: Watch Every Command Run
points: set -x (xtrace) prints every command to stderr AFTER expansion, prefixed by the PS4 string, just before it runs
Mnemonic: set -x turns xtrace ON, set +x turns it OFF — the flag letters follow set's on/off convention
The trace shows post-expansion reality: variables already substituted, globs already matched — you see exactly what executed
Core technique: diff the traced line against your source line; the difference IS the bug
Scope it: place set -x around a suspicious block and set +x after it — surgical tracing in large scripts
set -v prints each input line BEFORE expansion — run set -vx to see before and after side by side
Traces propagate into subshells and command substitutions: you get nested, indented traces for free
Capture a full run: bash -x script.sh 2> trace.log keeps stdout clean for piping the script's real output
BASH_XTRACEFD=9 (after exec 9> trace.log) routes xtrace to a dedicated file descriptor
Security caveat: -x expands secrets — passwords and API keys end up verbatim in logs; never leave tracing on in prod
Performance: tracing inside a 100k-iteration loop buries the signal and slows execution; trace sections instead
Zero-edit start: run bash -x script.sh args from outside the script for a first look

chapters.title: PS4: Trace Output That Tells You Where
points: PS4 is the prompt string prefixed to every xtrace line; the default is just '+ ', which tells you nothing
Set PS4='+ $BASH_SOURCE:$LINENO: ' near the top of the script to stamp every trace with file and line
$LINENO inside PS4 resolves at trace time to the line about to run — the single most useful debugging variable
Compact tag: PS4='+ L$LINENO: ' gives greppable markers like + L42: that map straight back to source
Full provenance: PS4='+ ${BASH_SOURCE}:${LINENO}: ${FUNCNAME[0]:-main}() ' shows file, line, and current function
Bash repeats the FIRST character of PS4 once per call depth — traces self-indent to reveal nesting and recursion
Timing traces: embed $EPOCHREALTIME (bash 5+) in PS4 to timestamp every line and expose slow spots
Export PS4 and SHELLOPTS=xtrace to push tracing down into scripts invoked by your script
PS4 affects only trace output, never script behavior — a debug-grade PS4 is safe to leave committed
Set a good PS4 in ~/.bashrc too, so every ad-hoc bash -x run in your terminal gets line numbers automatically
When a nested trace is unreadable, grep the PS4 line-number tag for the function name first, then read outward

chapters.title: trap ERR and trap DEBUG: Automatic Post-Mortems
points: trap 'handler' ERR runs handler whenever a simple command fails — an automatic error hook for the whole script
Canonical handler: cleanup() { echo FAILED at line $1 >&2; } installed with trap 'cleanup $LINENO' ERR
$LINENO passed into the handler pinpoints the failing line — free stack-trace-like post-mortem on every crash
Backtrace trick: print ${FUNCNAME[@]} inside the ERR handler to dump the function call chain that led here
trap DEBUG fires BEFORE every command: print $LINENO there for a full execution log (too heavy for routine use)
trap cleanup EXIT runs on every exit path — success, error, Ctrl-C — for temp files, locks, and rollback
Standard pairing: trap cleanup EXIT plus trap 'err $LINENO' ERR — errors get located, cleanup still always runs
Blind spot: the ERR trap does NOT fire for commands in if/while conditions or && / || chains — failure is expected there
set -E (errtrace) makes the ERR trap fire inside functions and subshells — enable it or handlers silently skip those
Traps reset in subshells: command substitution gets no parent trap unless set -E is on
Inspect and remove: trap -p ERR prints the active handler; trap - ERR uninstalls it
Handler hygiene: keep it short, write to stderr, and avoid recursion — a failing handler inside an ERR trap is misery

chapters.title: Strict Mode: set -euo pipefail
points: set -e (errexit): exit immediately when any command fails — fail fast instead of letting errors cascade
set -u (nounset): referencing an unset variable is an error — catches $OUTPT-style typos instantly
set -o pipefail: a pipeline's status is the FIRST non-zero, so failing_cmd | grep ... finally fails
Standard header for any non-trivial script: set -euo pipefail (optionally harden IFS to newline and tab only)
Documented holes: set -e ignores commands inside if/while conditions, && / || lists, and command substitution in assignments
Deliberate exemption: cmd || true continues on failure — always comment why, or you have rebuilt the silent bug
Best combo: set -euo pipefail PLUS trap ERR — -e stops the script, the trap logs exactly which line killed it
Gotcha: ((count++)) returns status 1 when count is 0 (result 0 is false) and kills -e scripts; use count=$((count+1))
Gotcha: a bare read returns non-zero at EOF — under -e a trailing read can kill the script, while-loop conditions are exempt
Arrays under set -u: bash 4.4+ handles empty arrays; older bash needs the ${arr[@]+${arr[@]}} expansion
pipefail payoff: curl -sf $url | grep pat now fails the pipeline when curl 404s instead of grep quietly passing on empty input
Trade-off: strict mode is brittle but predictable — add it to every new script from line one, retrofit legacy gradually

chapters.title: Field Guide: Common Silent-Failure Patterns
points: Pattern: VAR=$(cmd) discards cmd's failure — capture status instead: if ! VAR=$(cmd); then handle; fi
Pattern: missing cd guard — write cd $DIR || exit 1, or every later command runs in the wrong directory (the classic rm * disaster)
Pattern: cron's PATH is /usr/bin:/bin only — commands that work in your shell vanish there; set PATH at the top or use absolute paths
Pattern: curl writes the error page to your output file and exits 0 on HTTP errors — use curl -f so 404/500 actually fail
Pattern: grep exits 1 on no match — that is a FAILURE under set -e; branch deliberately with if grep -q pat file; then
Pattern: rm -rf $1/* with an empty or missing $1 — force required args with : ${1:?usage: need a directory}
Pattern: cp src dest where dest is not a directory silently OVERWRITES dest; write cp src dest/ to assert it is a directory
Pattern: for f in $(ls) breaks on spaces and newlines — iterate globs (for f in *) or find -print0 | xargs -0
Pattern: [ $a = $b ] with empty vars becomes [ = b ] — a syntax error masquerading as a value mismatch; quote both sides
Pattern: running with sh instead of bash silently drops bashisms — arrays, [[ ]], and local quirks break in confusing ways
Pattern: echo debug output vanishes in cron (no TTY) — log via logger to syslog or always >&2 to a redirected stderr
Detection habit: run any flaky script under bash -x once and read the LAST trace line — it is usually the crime scene

chapters.title: bashdb: Stepping Through with a Real Debugger
points: bashdb is a source-level debugger for bash: real breakpoints, stepping, and inspection — install the bashdb package
Start it with bashdb script.sh; you get a gdb-style prompt driving your script line by line
Core stepping: s steps INTO calls, n steps OVER them, c continues, finish runs to the end of the current function
Breakpoints: b 20 breaks at line 20, b funcname breaks at function entry, info breakpoints lists them all
print $var (or print ${arr[@]}) evaluates any expression at a breakpoint — inspect state without littering echo
Conditional breakpoints: cond 1 $count -gt 3 makes breakpoint 1 fire only when the condition holds
where prints the current function call stack — the true backtrace that trap ERR can only approximate
list shows surrounding source; frame up/down walks the stack; display var auto-prints after every step
run re-executes the script from the top inside the same session — edit, save, run, keep your breakpoints
Choose bashdb over set -x when you need to STOP and interrogate state; choose -x for a fast where-did-it-go-wrong
Limitations: bashdb tracks specific bash versions (mismatches misbehave) and needs WSL/MSYS on Windows
Muscle memory worth building: b, n, s, c, print, where covers 90 percent of interactive sessions

chapters.title: Choosing Tools, Logging in Production, and the Checklist
points: Escalation order: bash -n and shellcheck first (free, static), then a set -x trace, then bashdb when you must stop and inspect
Toolbox map: syntax → bash -n; code smells → shellcheck; flow → set -x + PS4; failure location → trap ERR; deep logic → bashdb
Production tracing: exec 9>>app.trace then BASH_XTRACEFD=9 — traces land in a file, never in a customer response
Build a DEBUG logger: debug() { [[ ${VERBOSE:-} ]] && echo [DEBUG] $* >&2 || true; } — flip verbosity with an env var, no re-editing
Watch live while capturing: cmd | tee out.log; the script(1) utility records whole terminal sessions for replay
Guard debug sessions: timeout and flock keep an interactive debugging run from wedging locks or shared resources
Keep a snippet library: strict header, ERR trap with backtrace, debug-grade PS4, VERBOSE logger — paste, do not retype
Cost model: static checks are near-free; xtrace costs one write per command; trap DEBUG fires before EVERY command — reserve it
Log safety: trace with a LINENO-only PS4 in shared environments; full -x leaks variable values (and secrets) into logs
Team standard: every non-trivial script ships with set -euo pipefail, an ERR trap, and a shellcheck-clean CI status
The checklist: bash -n? shellcheck? bash -x once? read the LAST trace line? check $? at each step? bashdb if still stuck?
Closing summary: bash is silent by default; everything here — xtrace, PS4, traps, strict mode, shellcheck, bashdb — exists to make it loud
